html:
The big picture

This lecture turns the language-independent ideas of 1 Foundations of Programming into running Python. Python sits on a layer stack — your program, the standard library and the interpreter, which hides the operating system and hardware and makes programs platform-independent. You can use it interactively (type an expression, see its value) or run a program file with python3 First.py. Running a file goes through a fixed pipeline: read the source → split it into tokens → parse them into a syntax tree → compile to bytecode → execute on a stack-based virtual machine. Finally, Python's layout rules matter more than in most languages: indentation is part of the syntax and defines which statements belong together.

History of Python — timeline of key milestones

Late 1980s: Guido van Rossum began working on Python as a successor to ABC.

1991: Python 0.9.0 released

  • Exception handling, functions, and the core data types (list, dict, str).

1994: Python 1.0: first official release.

  • lambda, map, filter, and reduce functions.

2000: Python 2.0:

  • list comprehensions, garbage collection, and support for Unicode.
  • Python Software Foundation (PSF) was established to manage the open-source development of Python.

2008: Python 3.0:

  • Major release that aimed to fix design flaws in the language
  • Not backward compatible with Python 2.x.

2010s: Growing adoption:

  • Python's popularity surged due to its ease of use in web development, scientific computing, data analysis, artificial intelligence, and more.

2020: Python 2.7 end of life:

  • Official support for Python 2 ended, encouraging the full transition to Python 3.

2021: Python 3.9 released:

  • Introduced features like dictionary merge & update operators, new string methods, and type hinting improvements.
Unclear (slides 31–32) — two dates
  • The Python Software Foundation was founded on 6 March 2001, not in 2000 (Python 2.0 did come out in 2000).
  • Python 3.9.0 was released on 5 October 2020, not in 2021.

Neither affects anything else in the course.

Common mistake — Python 2 code examples

"Not backward compatible" has a practical side: old tutorials and forum answers are often written in Python 2 and fail in Python 3. The most visible difference is print "Hello" (Python 2, a statement) versus print("Hello") (Python 3, a function call). If a copied example fails with a SyntaxError on a print line, that's usually why.

Python architecture

Python program on top of the standard library and the Python interpreter (download from www.python.org), which sits on the operating system and the hardware. A C program can reach the interpreter via the Python API.

  • The Python program is executed by the interpreter.
  • An extensive standard library is provided which the program can use.
  • Python can be extended by or used by C programs via the Python API.
  • The interpreter abstracts from the operating system and the hardware → platform independence.

Source: Johannes Ernesti, Peter Kaiser: Python 3 – Das umfassende Handbuch. 7th edition, Rheinwerk Verlag, 2023.

Intuition — what "platform independence" really means

Your .py file never talks to Windows, macOS or the processor directly; it only talks to the interpreter. So the same file runs everywhere — as long as an interpreter for that platform exists. The interpreter itself is a native, platform-specific program (that's why python.org offers different downloads for each system). It's the hybrid picture from 1 Foundations of Programming: platform-independent bytecode, platform-specific virtual machine.

Using Python

After installation, Python can be used interactively or program based.

Interactively (after typing python3 in a terminal):

mhitz@Trieste Programs % python3
Python 3.12.4 (v3.12.4:8e8a4baf65, Jun  6 2024, 17:33:18) [Clang 13.0.0 (clang-1300.0.29.30)] on darwin
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> 3 + 7**2 * (5 - 4)
52
>>> pi = 3.1415
>>> 12**2 * pi
452.37600000000003
>>> _ * 30
13571.28
>>> print("Bye!")
Bye!
>>>

The slide annotates the session:

  • 3 + 7**2 * (5 - 4) — an expression; 52 — the result of its evaluation
  • pi = 3.1415 — variable assignment; 12**2 * pi — variable use
  • _ holds the last evaluation result
  • print("Bye!") — invoking (calling) a function (subroutine); print() outputs its argument(s) on the console

Program based: the same kind of code saved in a file (First.py, below) and run with python3 First.py.

Unclear (slide 34)

The slide's subtitle reads "DONEC QUIS NUNC". That's placeholder (lorem ipsum) text left in the template, not content.

Why is 12**2 * pi not exactly 452.376?

Computers store float values in binary, and most decimal fractions (like 0.1, or the .1415 in pi) have no exact binary form, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form. So 3.1415 is stored as the nearest binary value, and the tiny difference shows up in the last digit of the result: 452.37600000000003. The same effect gives 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004. It's not a bug in Python; every language that uses standard floating-point numbers behaves this way. So don't compare floats with == when the values come from calculations.

Common mistake — _ in a program file

_ holding the last result is a feature of the interactive prompt only. In a program run with python3 First.py, nothing is stored in _ automatically — there _ is just an ordinary (and unusual) variable name. The same goes for results being shown: the prompt displays the value of every expression, while a program shows only what you print() (2 Python).

A first Python program — calculate the area of a circle for a given radius

# Calculate the area of a circle for a given radius

r = 12.3
a = 3.14159 * r * r
print("Area of a circle with radius", r, "=", a)

Output on the terminal window:

Area of a circle with radius 12.3 = 475.29115110000004

The slide labels each part:

  • # Calculate … — comment, ignored by the compiler; blank lines are also ignored by the compiler.
  • r, a — variables; r = 12.3 — assignment; 12.3 — a (floating point) number (literal).
  • 3.14159 * r * r — use of variables: reading their content. An expression consists of operands (variables, literals, function evaluations, …), operators (+, -, *, /, …) and parentheses (()).
  • "Area of a circle with radius" — text string (string literal).
  • print() is a function (or subroutine) – it displays the values given in parentheses (its arguments) in the console window: output on the terminal window.

We do not explain functions in detail for the time being – we simply regard them as »commands« that achieve a certain effect or as sub-expressions that yield a certain value.

Intuition — how print builds the line

print receives four separate arguments — a string, the value of r, the string "=" and the value of a — and writes them one after another, separated by one space, then ends the line. That's why there is a space before and after = in the output, although the strings don't contain one. Numbers don't need converting here, because each argument is printed on its own; the + approach from 3 Variables would need str().

Implementation without IDE

Create your program text

  • Use any text editor
  • Save as ProgramName.py – source code (here: First.py)

Compile and execute your program

  • python3 ProgramName.py (here: python3 First.py)
  • generates the compiled version of the program (bytecode) and executes (interprets) it
  • Admire results…
mhitz@Trieste Programs % python3 First.py
Area of a circle with radius 12.3 = 475.29115110000004
mhitz@Trieste Programs %

What happens in detail? (in the case of python3)

Interpreter initialization: The python3 command starts the Python interpreter. The interpreter initializes its internal data structures and prepares the runtime environment. This includes setting up memory management, importing built-in modules, and initializing the internal state.

Source code reading: The interpreter opens the specified source file (.py) and reads its contents into memory.

Lexical analysis (tokenization): The source code is converted into a stream of tokens. This step involves breaking down the code into meaningful components like keywords, identifiers, operators, literals, and punctuation.

Parsing: The token stream is analyzed according to the syntax rules of the Python language. This step constructs an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), which is a hierarchical representation of the program structure.

Compilation: The AST is compiled into Python bytecode. Bytecode is a low-level, platform-independent representation of the source code that the Python interpreter can execute. The bytecode is stored in .pyc files in the __pycache__ directory for future use, so the next time the script is run, it can skip the parsing and compilation steps if the source code hasn't changed.

Execution: The Python interpreter executes the bytecode using a stack-based virtual machine. This involves the following steps:

  • Loading constants and variables: The interpreter loads any constants and initializes variables.
  • Executing instructions: The interpreter fetches and executes bytecode instructions one by one. These instructions can include operations like arithmetic calculations, function calls, object manipulation, and flow control.
  • Managing function calls: When a function call is encountered, the interpreter sets up a new stack frame for the function's execution context and handles the transfer of control.

Importing modules: If the source file imports any external modules, the interpreter locates and loads these modules. This may involve reading additional .py files, compiling them to bytecode if necessary, and executing their top-level code to initialize the module.

Error handling: If any errors or exceptions occur during execution (such as syntax errors, runtime errors, or exceptions), the interpreter handles them according to the defined error-handling mechanisms. This includes printing stack traces and error messages to the console.

Program termination: After the last instruction of the source file is executed, the interpreter performs any necessary cleanup, such as closing files and releasing resources. The program then terminates.

Java is also an interpreted language with a similar execution process. In C and C++, on the other hand, the source code is compiled into the machine code of the target platform, which is then loaded into memory and executed autonomously (without an interpreter).

Worked example — the pipeline on one line of First.py

Follow a = 3.14159 * r * r through the steps:

  1. Tokenize — cut the text into meaningful pieces: a (name), = (operator), 3.14159 (number), * (operator), r (name), *, r. Spaces disappear here; they only separate tokens.
  2. Parse — arrange the tokens by the grammar into a tree: an assignment whose target is a and whose value is the product (3.14159 * r) * r. Operator precedence and left-to-right grouping are decided at this step.
  3. Compile — turn the tree into bytecode instructions for the stack machine, roughly: push 3.14159, push the value of r, multiply, push r again, multiply, store the result in a.
  4. Execute — the virtual machine runs those instructions.

A typo breaks the pipeline at a specific step: a = 3.14159 * * r tokenizes fine but can't be parsed — a syntax error, reported before anything runs.

Intuition — a stack-based virtual machine

The machine language in 1 Foundations of Programming had one accumulator register. Python's virtual machine instead uses a stack: operations take their inputs from the top of the stack and put the result back there. 10 \cdot 6 + 7 becomes: push 10, push 6, multiply (pops both, pushes 60), push 7, add (pops both, pushes 67). No register names are needed, which is part of what keeps the bytecode platform-independent.

Will python3 First.py leave a First.pyc behind?

No. CPython caches bytecode in __pycache__ only for imported modules. The file you run directly is compiled into memory each time and not saved. So the "next time the script is run" on slide 38 applies to modules your program imports, not to First.py itself. For small scripts compiling takes a fraction of a second anyway; the cache pays off for large libraries that are imported again and again.

Connection

Syntax errors are found while parsing (nothing runs), runtime errors only while executing. The prep course's 2 Python showed both kinds; this pipeline shows where each one comes from.

A first Python program – variation: calculate the area of a circle for any radius

# Calculate the area of a circle for any radius

inp = input("Radius: ")
r = float(inp)
a = 3.14159 * r * r
print("Area of a circle with radius", r, "=", a)

Changes to the previous example are marked in red: the two lines with input and float.

mhitz@Trieste Programs % python3 First.py
Radius: 3
Area of a circle with radius 3.0 = 28.274309999999996
mhitz@Trieste Programs %
  • input() is another function – it displays its argument in the console window and reads and returns a text entered by the user.
  • float() is a function that converts the text given into a floating point value (if possible).
Why is the float() line needed at all?

input() always returns a string, even when the user types digits: the text "3", not the number 3. A string can't be multiplied by a float, so 3.14159 * inp * inp would stop with a TypeError. float(inp) converts the text to the number 3.0. That's also why the output says radius 3.0: r is now a float.

Common mistake — typing a decimal comma

On an Austrian or German keyboard it's natural to type 2,5. But float("2,5") fails with ValueError: could not convert string to float: '2,5'. Python only accepts a decimal point: 2.5. The same applies to number literals in code: r = 2,5 doesn't fail, but it silently creates a pair of two numbers, not 2.5.

Visual design of Python programs

Text elements ignored by the compiler/interpreter

Comments are used to explain the program. Two flavors:

# After this symbol, everything up to the end of the line is ignored

""" Comments between pairs of three quotation marks can span
    any number of lines """

Blank lines structure the program vertically and can be used at will.

Spaces or tabs structure the program horizontally – this must reflect the logical structure (they are not ignored by the system).

In Python, the horizontal indenting reflects the logical structure of the program. In many other languages (Java, C, C++ …), this structure is defined by parentheses (usually { }), and indenting is ignored by the compiler.

Intuition — the triple-quoted "comment" is really a string

Technically, """ … """ creates a string literal that is simply not used, so it has no effect — which is why it can serve as a multi-line comment. Placed as the first line of a function, the same string becomes its docstring, the built-in documentation that help() shows. Real comments (#) disappear already at the tokenize step.

Indenting

Statements in Python may consist of a statement header an[d] a statement body:

StatementHeader:
    SubStatement
    …               ← statement body
    SubStatement

Horizontal indenting is mandatory and must be consistent (either blanks or tabs).

PythonC, C++, Java
# Make sure a ≤ b:
if a > b:
h = a
a = b
b = h		// Make sure a ≤ b (in C, C++, Java)
if (a > b) {
int h = a;
a = b;
b = h;
}

In C, C++ and Java, horizontal indenting is usual, but ignored by the compiler.

Worked example — what the swap does, and why it needs h

Goal: make sure a ≤ b. Start with a = 7, b = 3.

  1. Test: 7 > 3 is true, so the indented body runs.
  2. Save a before it's overwritten: h = 7.
  3. Copy b into a: a = 3.
  4. Restore the saved value into b: b = 7.

Now a = 3, b = 7 ✓. Without h, step 3 would destroy the 7 for good — the same trap as in the prep course's code challenge (2 Python). If a is already ≤ b, the test is false and none of the three indented lines runs: indentation alone decides that all three belong to the if.

Common mistake — indentation errors
  • Indenting a line that doesn't open a block, or indenting deeper than the line above, gives IndentationError: unexpected indent.
  • Forgetting to indent after a line ending in : gives IndentationError: expected an indented block.
  • Mixing tabs and spaces in one block gives TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation — even when it looks aligned in your editor. Pick one (the convention is 4 spaces) and let the editor insert it.

Merging & splitting lines

Statements can be merged into one line

  • if the body contains only one sub-statement:

    if a > b: print("a greater than b")

  • if the (> 1) sub-statements are separated by semicolons:

    # Make sure a ≤ b:
if a > b: h = a; a = b; b = h

Statements can be split into multiple lines

  • inside parentheses:

    print("I am a",
      "single statement")

  • using a backslash (\) as the last character before the line break:

    print \
    ("I am a single statement")
Intuition — which one to prefer

Both merging tricks make code harder to read, so use them rarely. For splitting, prefer the parentheses: while a bracket is open, Python knows the statement isn't finished. The backslash is fragile: it must be the very last character, and an invisible space after it turns it into a syntax error.
